analysis.one_liner: Redirects Social Security payroll taxes into personal stock-and-bond accounts and gradually raises the retirement age.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have moved a share of every worker's Social Security payroll tax into a government-run fund, then into a personal retirement account the worker could direct, invested in broad stock and bond index funds through approved mutual fund companies. To offset the diverted money, it would have trimmed guaranteed benefits for future retirees, gradually raised the retirement age past 67, and covered newly hired state and local workers. It also would have let the government keep Social Security surpluses out of general spending and use them to pay down the national debt, while ending the rule that reduces benefits for beneficiaries who keep working.
analysis.who_benefits: Future retirees who elect accounts would own bequeathable savings invested in stock and bond index funds, could get a tax deduction of up to $1,000 (50% of voluntary contributions up to $2,000), and could work past retirement age without losing benefits. Widows and widowers would see benefits increase. Approved mutual fund companies would gain a new stream of accounts and fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Future retirees electing accounts; mutual fund companies

how_it_helps.text: Workers and spouses could direct deposits into personal retirement savings accounts once their interim balance reached $2,500, and accounts pass to the holder's estate as a lump sum at death [S3].
Account money would be invested in broad stock and bond index portfolios (default 60/40, with 40/60 and 80/20 options) managed by firms approved by the Treasury [S3].
Account holders could deduct 50% of voluntary contributions up to $2,000 a year, whether or not they itemize, and account deposits would be excluded from income [S2].

The bill would eliminate the earnings test that reduces benefits for beneficiaries at retirement age who keep working, increase widow's and widower's benefits, and accelerate delayed-retirement credits [S2].
Social Security surpluses would be transferred to the trust fund and automatically sequestered from other federal spending to reduce debt held by the public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The transition is expensive: the Treasury would deposit, from the general fund, an amount equal to 100% of the redirected payroll taxes of every covered worker, plus $11 billion to $165 billion a year into the trust fund through 2009 [S2, S3]. Meanwhile the guaranteed benefit is reduced: the primary insurance amount would be cut by the value of the account deposits assuming 3.7% interest, the benefit formula is made less generous over time (up to a 17% reduction for higher earners by 2014), and the retirement age rises gradually beyond 67 [S3]. Workers also bear market risk on their accounts, since the benefit offset is fixed regardless of how their investments perform.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers via the general fund; future retirees' benefits

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed benefits would shrink: the benefit formula would pay a smaller share of earnings each year, reaching reductions of up to 17% for higher earners by 2014, and monthly benefits would be reduced by the annuity value of every dollar deposited into an account [S3].
The retirement age and early retirement age would rise gradually beyond current law, so people would have to work longer or accept bigger early-filing reductions [S2].

The transition is expensive: the general fund would replace 100% of the redirected payroll taxes plus $829 billion in specified trust-fund transfers from 2001 through 2009, a large new claim on the rest of the budget [S3].

Accounts carry market risk while the offset to guaranteed benefits assumes a fixed 3.7% return, so a worker whose investments do poorly would end up with both a smaller check and a smaller account than promised [S3].
Newly hired state and local employees would be pulled into Social Security coverage, changing arrangements many state pension systems currently rely on [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real gains to some workers — personal ownership, bequeathable accounts, an end to the retirement earnings test — but it paid for them largely by trimming the guaranteed benefit formula, raising the retirement age, and drawing roughly $830 billion-plus from the general fund during the transition, while exposing retirees to market risk against a fixed-offset formula. Honest supporters would acknowledge the bill protected current retirees while shifting both risk and financing burden onto younger workers and the rest of the budget.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never came up for a vote before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Smith of Michigan introduced the bill on November 3, 1999, joined by seven original cosponsors, six Republicans and one Democrat (Rep. Charlie Stenholm) [S3].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Budget Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
On November 15, 1999, it was sent to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, where no markup or vote ever followed [S5].
The only later action in the record was the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 26, 2000; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing Social Security benefit formula, retirement ages, and payroll-tax financing were left untouched, which favored those who wanted to preserve the current system. The mutual fund and investment management industry lost the chance at a large new mandated stream of accounts and fees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defenders of the existing Social Security system

for.name: Rep. Nick Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the floor in June 2000.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction (Reps. Porter, Kolbe, Campbell, Sanford, Shadegg, Toomey).

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making the sponsorship bipartisan.

sides.party_line_note: The eight named sponsors split seven Republicans and one Democrat, and the bill never advanced far enough to attract recorded opposition votes.

industries.industry: Mutual fund and investment management firms
industries.note: Personal accounts could only be held at Treasury-approved regulated investment companies tracking broad stock and bond indexes, and the interim fund would hire contracted investment managers — the bill would have made approved fund companies the mandatory channel for redirected Social Security taxes and a new source of fees. Workers would own the accounts, but the industry would be locked in as the permanent gatekeeper.

industries.industry: State and local government pension systems
industries.note: Newly hired state and local employees would be brought under Social Security coverage, reducing the pool of workers in stand-alone public pension plans.
Covered employers would face new excise-tax accounting tied to the reallocation percentage and reporting tied to the new accounts, while the bill explicitly bars any payroll tax increase.
